nameStory: The Brickwork Woodlouse gets its name from the distinctive pattern on its back that resembles the mortar lines between bricks on a building. When you look closely at this little crustacean, you'll see pale lines creating a grid-like pattern across its dark body segments, just like looking at the side of a brick wall.
description: The Brickwork Woodlouse is a small, armored crustacean that looks like a tiny armadillo scuttling around in your garden. These oval-shaped creatures are about half an inch long and have segmented bodies with seven pairs of legs. They're actually more closely related to shrimp and lobsters than to insects, despite living on land. Like their marine cousins, they breathe through gills and need moisture to survive.

idTips.label: Brick-like pattern
idTips.description: Look for pale yellowish lines running across the dark gray body segments, creating a distinctive grid pattern that really does look like tiny brickwork

idTips.label: Spiny front corners
idTips.description: The front corners of the head have small but noticeable spiny projections that feel slightly prickly if you gently touch them with a finger

idTips.label: Rolling ability
idTips.description: Unlike pill bugs, these woodlice can only partially roll up when disturbed, forming more of a loose C-shape than a tight ball

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: The shell feels smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, not bumpy or granular like some other woodlice species

idTips.label: Antennae length
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae with the outer pair being noticeably longer, constantly tapping and exploring as they move

habitat: You'll find Brickwork Woodlice in moist, sheltered spots around homes and gardens throughout New England. Look under flower pots, logs, leaf litter, and mulch, especially in areas that stay damp but drain well. They're particularly common around foundations, compost piles, and garden beds where they can find both moisture and decaying plant matter to eat.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and stones. Look for them during mild, humid days when they're most active.
seasonality.summer: Most easily found during summer months when they're actively foraging. Check under objects during the day, or use a flashlight at night to spot them moving around openly.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper shelter. Often found in larger groups gathering under particularly good hiding spots as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, mulch, or other insulated spots where they become dormant. Rarely seen unless you dig into their winter refuges on warmer days.

funFact: Brickwork Woodlice are actually ocean refugees - their ancestors lived in the sea millions of years ago, and they still carry their ocean heritage in their blood, which contains copper-based hemocyanin that turns blue when oxygenated, just like their lobster and crab relatives!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Common Rough Woodlice, but the Brickwork's distinctive pale grid pattern is the dead giveaway - think 'brick pattern equals Brickwork Woodlouse.' Also distinguished from pill bugs (roly-polies) because Brickwork Woodlice can't roll into a complete ball.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bugs,' woodlice aren't insects at all - they're crustaceans that never fully adapted to land life. This is why you'll never find them in truly dry places, and why they're most active on humid nights when the air feels almost oceanic.
compareHints: The Brickwork Woodlouse differs from its close relative, the Common Rough Woodlouse, primarily in its distinctive pale brick-like pattern and the prominent spiny projections on its front corners. While Common Rough Woodlice have a more uniformly mottled gray appearance with a rougher texture, Brickwork Woodlice have that telltale geometric pattern and smoother feel.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The main relative in New England is the brickwork woodlouse, but rough woodlice are much more common and widespread.
